patient_information: A 55-year-old Swiss couple, both fitness instructors, previously healthy.
chief_complaint: The husband developed a fever (39°C, 102.2°F), myalgias, generalized weakness, and shortness of breath with oxygen desaturation and bilateral interstitial infiltrates over 4 days. Three weeks later, his wife presented with similar complaints, rapidly deteriorating into cardiorespiratory failure and multi-organ failure.
history_of_present_illness: The husband developed a fever, myalgias, and generalized weakness during their flight back to Switzerland, 4 days before presentation at the hospital. He continued to be febrile, too weak to walk unassisted or hold up a newspaper, and developed shortness of breath with oxygen desaturation and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The following day, he was transferred to the intensive care unit for non-invasive ventilator support. Three weeks later, his wife presented with similar complaints and was admitted to the same hospital, rapidly deteriorating over 24 hours after admission with cardiorespiratory failure, multi-organ failure requiring hemodialysis, and profuse bleeding from puncture sites in the context of disseminated intravascular coagulation.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The couple travelled for 3 months from Ecuador to Chile, spending the last month hiking, camping, and taking occasional mud baths in the Chile-Argentinian border region. The mode of transmission remained unclear; both human-to-human-transmission and acquisition from a common source were possible. Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS) is caused by Andesvirus (ANDV), a New World hantavirus endemic in the border region between Chile and Argentina, with infection typically occurring through inhalation of excreta from the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus). Outdoor activities are the major risk factor for acquiring ANDV infection.
vitals: Husband: BP 90/55 mmHg, pulse 120 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on ambient air, and temperature 39°C (102.2°F). Wife on admission (3 weeks after her husband's admission): normal blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation, temperature 38.6°C (101.5°F).
physical_exam: Husband: No abnormal findings on cardiopulmonary auscultation. Wife: No abnormal findings on auscultation.
labs_and_diagnostics: Husband, on admission: WCC 7.3 G/L (reference: 3.0-10.5), 35% band neutrophils; platelets 48 G/L (reference: 150-450); CRP 68 mg/L (reference: <5); glomerular filtration rate >90 mL/min (reference: >90 mL/min); transaminases normal. Chest x-ray at presentation showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Respiratory pathogen panel (including influenza A/B, parainfluenza, RSV, adenovirus, rhinovirus, bocavirus, coronavirus and human metapneumovirus) from a nasopharyngeal swab came back negative. HIV test negative. Wife, on admission: WCC 1.88 G/L; platelets 98 G/L; CRP 7 mg/L; glomerular filtration rate >90 mL/min; transaminases normal. Chest radiography at presentation was normal, but during the course of the disease she developed extensive bilateral infiltrates with pleural effusions. Both patients were confirmed by PCR and serology to be infected with Andesvirus (ANDV). Computed tomography of the chest (lung window) of the female patient on day 13 showed extensive and dense dorsal infiltrations and the centrally placed ECMO cannulae.
differential_diagnosis: Conditions that may present with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and possible multi-organ failure after travel to South America include influenza and other respiratory viruses, New World hantaviruses, pneumococcal pneumonia, Rickettsial diseases (Rickettsia rickettsiae, scrub typhus), pulmonary plague, fungal infections (Histoplasmosis, Cryptococcosis), and severe malaria. Most viral haemorrhagic fevers (yellow fever, dengue and the New World arenaviruses, e.g. Junín virus and Machupo virus) can be excluded based on incubation time being well below 21 days, with hantavirus infections being the only exception (incubation time up to 35 days).
management_and_clinical_course: Both patients should be referred to a tertiary care setting equipped to handle ARDS and haemorrhagic fevers. Clinically, securing cardiorespiratory function is the main priority. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are indicated as empirical treatment until further results are back. A patient with respiratory symptoms must be treated under standard hygiene and droplet precautions (at least) to prevent potential nosocomial transmission; airborne precautions may be required. The husband was treated with non-invasive ventilation for 5 days and made a full recovery after a month of rehabilitation. His wife experienced a dramatic course with nearly a full month on ECMO treatment, multi-organ failure requiring renal replacement therapy, and haemorrhagic complications with mass transfusions of blood products. Bleeding complications at the inguinal ECMO insertion sites (compartment syndrome and leg ischemia) required central ECMO replacement. Additional bleeding complications at inguinal and thoracic insertion sites required several surgical interventions. Nosocomial infections followed, and she remained in intensive care for 5 months and an additional 12 months in rehabilitation.
final_diagnosis: Both patients were confirmed to be infected with Andesvirus (ANDV), a New World species of the family Hantaviridae, causing Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS). The diagnosis was supported by positive PCR and serology results for ANDV, along with their travel history to the Chile-Argentinian border region where ANDV is endemic, and their clinical presentation of ARDS and multi-organ failure.
